questions.s: Two monosaccharide units in a disaccharide are joined by a
questions.e: A condensation reaction between hydroxyl groups of two sugars forms a glycosidic bond and releases one water molecule. Peptide bonds join amino acids, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol and phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides.

questions.s: Complete hydrolysis of sucrose gives
questions.e: Sucrose (cane sugar) is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose unit. Glucose plus galactose is lactose, and two glucose units make maltose, which are the usual confusions.

questions.s: The high specific heat capacity of water, which keeps body temperature stable, is mainly due to
o: strong covalent bonds within each molecule
its ionisation into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions
questions.e: Much of the heat supplied to water is used to break hydrogen bonds between neighbouring polar molecules before the molecules can move faster, so temperature rises slowly. The O-H covalent bonds inside the molecule are not broken on heating, so they do not explain the effect.

questions.s: Cellulose differs from starch because cellulose is a polymer of
o: α-glucose joined by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds
β-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
questions.e: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose with β-1,4 links, which lets chains lie side by side and form strong microfibrils. Starch (amylose and amylopectin) is built from α-glucose, with α-1,6 branches only in amylopectin.

questions.s: A peptide bond is formed between
o: the R groups of two neighbouring amino acids
the amino groups of two amino acids
the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another
the carboxyl groups of two amino acids
questions.e: In condensation, the -COOH of one amino acid reacts with the -NH₂ of the next, releasing water and forming the -CO-NH- peptide link. R groups do not take part in forming the backbone bond.

questions.s: A single polypeptide chain of 50 amino acids is made by condensation. The number of water molecules released is
questions.e: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule, and a linear chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, so 50 − 1 = 49. Choosing 50 counts one bond per amino acid, forgetting that the two ends are free.

questions.s: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to
o: the sequence of amino acids in a chain
the association of two or more polypeptide chains
the coiling of a chain into an α-helix
the folding of a single chain into a compact 3-D shape
questions.e: Quaternary structure exists only when a protein has more than one polypeptide, as in haemoglobin with four chains. The amino acid sequence is primary structure, α-helix is secondary and the 3-D folding of one chain is tertiary.

questions.s: A triglyceride is formed when glycerol combines with
o: one fatty acid and two phosphates
questions.e: The three -OH groups of glycerol each form an ester bond with one fatty acid, releasing three water molecules. A phosphate group replaces one fatty acid only in a phospholipid, not in a triglyceride.

questions.s: In a phospholipid molecule, the part that is hydrophilic is the
questions.e: The charged phosphate group (often with choline) attracts water, while the two non-polar fatty acid tails repel it. This is why phospholipids form a bilayer with heads facing the watery sides and tails inside.

questions.s: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 18 % guanine. The percentage of adenine in it is
questions.e: By base pairing G = C = 18 %, so G + C = 36 % and A + T = 64 %; since A = T, adenine = 32 %. 64 % is A + T together, not adenine alone.

questions.s: Which of the following is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.e: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine and ribose in place of deoxyribose. Adenine occurs in both nucleic acids, while thymine and deoxyribose are features of DNA.

questions.s: Which pair of nitrogenous bases are both purines?
questions.e: Purines (adenine and guanine) have a double ring, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring. Adenine-thymine and guanine-cytosine are complementary pairs, each made of one purine and one pyrimidine.

questions.s: A conjugated molecule formed by the combination of a protein with a carbohydrate is a
questions.e: Glyco- refers to sugar, so a protein with a carbohydrate chain attached is a glycoprotein, common on cell surfaces. Lipoproteins carry lipid, nucleoproteins combine protein with nucleic acid, and a phospholipid contains no protein.

questions.s: The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was proposed by
questions.e: Emil Fischer (1894) suggested that the active site has a rigid shape exactly matching the substrate, like a key in a lock. Koshland later proposed the induced-fit model, in which the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds.

questions.s: According to the induced-fit model of enzyme action,
o: the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds
the active site is rigid and exactly fits the substrate's shape
the substrate binds anywhere on the enzyme surface
the enzyme is used up in the reaction
questions.e: Koshland's model says the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate, which strains bonds and helps the reaction. A rigid, exactly fitting active site is the older lock-and-key idea, and in both models the enzyme is not used up.

questions.s: A non-protein organic cofactor that is loosely attached to an enzyme during the reaction is called a
questions.e: Coenzymes such as NAD are organic and attach only loosely, so they can move between enzymes. A prosthetic group is also organic but tightly (often covalently) bound, activators are inorganic ions, and the apoenzyme is the protein part itself.

questions.s: Malonate resembles succinate and slows the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase. Its inhibiting effect can be reduced most effectively by
o: raising the temperature well above optimum
questions.e: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor: it competes with succinate for the active site, so adding more substrate makes it more likely that succinate, not malonate, occupies each active site. Heating far above optimum denatures the enzyme, and fewer enzyme molecules or heavy-metal ions only reduce activity further.

questions.s: A non-competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction because it
o: resembles the substrate and occupies the active site
breaks the peptide bonds of the enzyme permanently
binds only to the substrate molecules
binds a site other than the active site and alters the enzyme's shape
questions.e: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches to another (allosteric) site, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate cannot be converted; adding more substrate does not overcome it. Occupying the active site because of similar shape is how a competitive inhibitor works.

questions.s: In an enzyme reaction with a fixed amount of enzyme, the rate stops increasing at high substrate concentration because
o: the enzyme is denatured by excess substrate
all active sites are occupied at any moment
the product is no longer formed
questions.e: Once every active site is busy, extra substrate molecules have to wait for a free site, so the rate reaches a maximum and levels off. The enzyme is not denatured by substrate; to raise the rate further, more enzyme is needed.

questions.s: An enzyme extract with optimum 37 °C is held at 70 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled back to 37 °C. Its activity at 37 °C will be
o: very low, because its active site has been permanently changed
normal, because cooling back to 37 °C restores the original shape
higher than before, because it has been activated
normal, but only after more substrate is added
questions.e: High temperature breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the active site in shape, so the enzyme is denatured and does not refold on cooling. Low temperatures only inactivate enzymes temporarily, which is why expecting recovery on cooling is the common mistake.

questions.s: The cell theory, stating that all plants and animals are made of cells, was put forward mainly by
questions.e: Matthias Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Theodor Schwann (animals, 1839) proposed that cells are the basic units of living things. Watson and Crick described DNA structure, and the other two pairs proposed models of the cell membrane.

questions.s: The idea that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula e cellula) was added to the cell theory by
questions.e: Rudolf Virchow (1855) concluded that cells come only from the division of existing cells, ruling out spontaneous generation of cells. Robert Hooke first named cells in cork, and Robert Brown discovered the nucleus.

questions.s: An electron microscope can resolve much finer detail than a light microscope because
o: its lenses are made of better glass
electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
questions.e: Resolving power improves as the wavelength used becomes shorter, and an electron beam has a wavelength thousands of times shorter than light. Electron microscopes use electromagnetic lenses, not glass, and specimens must be dead and in a vacuum.

questions.s: The resolution (resolving power) of a microscope is its ability to
o: show two close points as separate
stain cell structures in different colours
questions.e: Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as distinct. Making an object look larger is magnification; magnifying without better resolution only gives a bigger blurred image.

questions.s: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by
questions.e: In 1972 Singer and Nicolson described the membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins float like tiles of a mosaic. Danielli and Davson had earlier proposed a protein-lipid-protein sandwich model.

questions.s: In the Danielli-Davson (sandwich) model, the cell membrane was described as
o: a lipid bilayer between two continuous layers of protein
globular proteins floating freely within a fluid lipid bilayer
a single layer of cellulose fibres
a protein layer between two lipid layers
questions.e: Danielli and Davson pictured a phospholipid bilayer coated on both sides by continuous protein sheets. The idea of proteins scattered in and floating through the bilayer is the later fluid mosaic model, which replaced it.

questions.s: The middle lamella that cements neighbouring plant cells together is mainly composed of
questions.e: The middle lamella forms first, between two daughter cells, and is made of calcium and magnesium pectates that hold the cells together. Cellulose makes up the primary and secondary walls laid down on either side of it, and lignin is added later to some secondary walls.

questions.s: The cell wall of most bacteria is made mainly of
questions.e: Bacterial walls are built from peptidoglycan, chains of sugars cross-linked by short peptides. Cellulose is the main wall material of plants and chitin that of most fungi, so these are the usual mix-ups.

questions.s: The folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called
questions.e: Cristae increase the surface area of the inner membrane, which carries the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. Thylakoids and grana belong to chloroplasts, and cisternae are the flattened sacs of the ER and Golgi apparatus.

questions.s: Which pair of organelles both contain their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes?
questions.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small circular DNA and prokaryote-like 70S ribosomes, which supports the endosymbiont idea of their origin. The Golgi, ER, lysosomes and peroxisomes have no DNA of their own.

questions.s: Ribosomal RNA is synthesised and ribosome subunits are assembled in the
questions.e: The nucleolus is the dense region of the nucleus where rRNA genes are transcribed and joined with proteins to make ribosome subunits, which then pass out through nuclear pores. The Golgi apparatus packages proteins but does not make ribosomes.

questions.s: In liver cells, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is especially important for
questions.e: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes; it makes lipids and steroids and, in liver cells, contains enzymes that detoxify drugs and alcohol. Protein synthesis for export is the job of rough ER, whose surface carries ribosomes.

questions.s: The organelle that modifies, sorts and packages proteins into secretory vesicles is the
questions.e: Proteins from the rough ER enter the Golgi apparatus, where they are modified (for example by adding sugars) and packed into vesicles for secretion or for lysosomes. Mitochondria make ATP and centrioles help form the spindle.

questions.s: The digestion of a cell's own worn-out organelles (autophagy) is carried out by
questions.e: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of hydrolytic enzymes that fuse with old organelles and digest them. Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes such as catalase that break down hydrogen peroxide, not whole organelles.

questions.s: The 80S ribosome of a eukaryotic cytoplasm is made of two subunits, which are
questions.e: Eukaryotic 80S ribosomes have a 60S large and a 40S small subunit. S values measure sedimentation rate and are not simply added, which is why 60S + 40S gives 80S; 50S and 30S are the subunits of the prokaryotic 70S ribosome.

questions.s: A cell of the pancreas that secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes would be expected to have a well-developed
o: rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus
smooth endoplasmic reticulum and many lysosomes
questions.e: Digestive enzymes are proteins made on ribosomes of the rough ER and then packaged for export by the Golgi apparatus. Smooth ER makes lipids, not proteins, so a secretory protein-making cell is rich in rough ER.

questions.s: In a chloroplast, the light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle take place respectively in the
o: outer membrane and the intermembrane space
questions.e: Chlorophyll and the electron carriers are in the thylakoid membranes (stacked as grana), where ATP and NADPH are made. The Calvin cycle enzymes are dissolved in the stroma, which uses that ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂; reversing the two is the common error.

questions.s: Which structure is present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.e: All cells make proteins, so all have ribosomes (70S in prokaryotes, 80S in the eukaryotic cytoplasm). Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, so they have no mitochondria, nuclear envelope or Golgi apparatus.

questions.s: The five-kingdom system of classification was proposed in 1969 by
questions.e: Whittaker placed organisms in Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, using cell type, level of organisation and mode of nutrition. Linnaeus used two kingdoms, Haeckel added a third (Protista) and Chatton introduced the prokaryote-eukaryote division.

questions.s: In the scientific name Mangifera indica (mango), written by binomial nomenclature, the word Mangifera is the name of the
questions.e: In the binomial system of Linnaeus the first word, written with a capital letter, is the genus and the second word, in small letters, is the species epithet. Family and order are higher ranks that do not appear in the two-word name.

questions.s: The protein coat that surrounds the nucleic acid of a virus is called the
questions.e: The capsid is made of protein subunits called capsomeres and encloses the viral DNA or RNA. Some viruses also have an outer lipid envelope taken from the host membrane, while a capsule and a cell wall are bacterial structures.

questions.s: In the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage, the final stage is
o: joining of the phage DNA into the host chromosome
division of the host cell carrying a prophage
lysis of the host cell, releasing many new phages
attachment of the phage tail to the host wall
questions.e: After the phage DNA takes over the cell and new phages are assembled, the host cell bursts (lyses) and releases them. Integration of phage DNA as a prophage and its copying during host division belong to the lysogenic cycle, and attachment is the first step.

questions.s: HIV weakens the immune system mainly by destroying
o: plasma B cells of the spleen
questions.e: HIV binds to the CD4 receptor found on helper T cells, multiplies inside them and kills them, so both cell-mediated and antibody responses fail. Red cells and platelets have no CD4 receptor and are not its target.

questions.s: A retrovirus such as HIV can insert its genes into host DNA because it carries the enzyme
questions.e: Reverse transcriptase uses the viral RNA as a template to make a DNA copy, which then becomes integrated into the host chromosome. Restriction enzymes cut DNA and come from bacteria, not retroviruses.

questions.s: Which type of viral hepatitis is spread mainly through contaminated food and water?
questions.e: Hepatitis A virus is shed in faeces and spreads by the faecal-oral route where sanitation is poor. Hepatitis B, C and D spread through blood and body fluids, such as unscreened transfusions and reused syringes.

questions.s: Rod-shaped bacteria are known as
questions.e: Bacteria are named by shape: bacilli are rods, cocci are spheres, spirilla are spirals and vibrios are comma-shaped. Cocci is the usual confusion because the words are often learned together.

questions.s: Gram-positive bacteria appear purple after Gram staining because they have
o: an outer lipid membrane that absorbs the safranin counterstain
a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet
questions.e: The thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria holds the crystal violet-iodine complex even after alcohol washing. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer under an outer membrane, lose the violet and take up the pink safranin counterstain.

questions.s: Endospores are formed by some bacteria mainly to
questions.e: One cell forms only one endospore, a tough, dormant structure resistant to heat and drying, which germinates when conditions improve. Because one cell gives one spore, it is a survival method, not reproduction, which is done by binary fission.

questions.s: In the cyanobacterium Nostoc, nitrogen fixation takes place in special thick-walled cells called
questions.e: Heterocysts lack the oxygen-producing photosystem and have thick walls, which protect the oxygen-sensitive enzyme nitrogenase. Akinetes are resting spores and hormogonia are short fragments used in reproduction.

questions.s: Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium, which is transmitted to humans by the bite of
questions.e: Only female mosquitoes suck blood, and Plasmodium completes part of its life cycle in the female Anopheles. Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue virus, not malaria.

questions.s: Which protist is correctly matched with its structure for locomotion?
questions.e: Paramecium beats thousands of short cilia, Amoeba moves by pseudopodia and Euglena uses a flagellum. Plasmodium is a non-motile parasite in most stages, so the other pairings swap or invent structures.

questions.s: The cell wall of most fungi is mainly composed of
questions.e: Fungal walls contain chitin, a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide also found in the exoskeleton of insects. Cellulose is the plant wall material and peptidoglycan is found in bacteria.

questions.s: A bacteriophage injects its DNA into a bacterium, but the cell does not burst; instead, all its descendants for many generations carry the phage DNA. This shows that the phage is in the
o: lytic cycle, at the assembly stage
questions.e: In lysogeny the phage DNA joins the host chromosome as a prophage and is copied with it at each division, so daughter cells inherit it without being destroyed. In the lytic cycle new phages are made at once and the host bursts within a short time.

questions.s: Prions, which cause diseases such as mad cow disease, are infectious particles made of
questions.e: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause normal copies of the same protein to misfold, and they contain no nucleic acid. Viroids, by contrast, are short naked RNA molecules, and viruses contain nucleic acid inside a protein coat.

questions.s: A bacterium with many flagella distributed all over its surface is described as
questions.e: Peritrichous means flagella around the whole cell. Monotrichous is a single flagellum, lophotrichous is a tuft at one end and amphitrichous is a flagellum or tuft at each end.

questions.s: Penicillin kills many bacteria but does not harm human cells because it
o: destroys the 80S ribosomes that are found only in bacterial cells
blocks the synthesis of peptidoglycan, which human cells lack
dissolves the nuclear membrane of bacteria
blocks the cellulose cell wall of bacteria
questions.e: Penicillin prevents the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing bacteria form weak walls and burst; human cells have no cell wall, so they are unaffected. Bacteria have 70S ribosomes and no nuclear membrane, and their walls are not made of cellulose.

questions.s: Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because they
o: live only in water as adults
live on land but need water for fertilisation
questions.e: Mosses and liverworts grow on land, but their sperms must swim through a film of water to reach the egg. They have no true vascular tissue and produce spores, not seeds.

questions.s: In the life cycle of a moss, the dominant, independent generation is the
questions.e: The leafy green moss plant is the haploid gametophyte; the sporophyte (foot, seta and capsule) grows on it and depends on it for food. A dominant sporophyte is the feature of ferns and seed plants, which is the usual confusion.

questions.s: In a fern such as Adiantum, the main leafy plant is the
questions.e: The fern plant with roots, rhizome and fronds is the diploid sporophyte, which bears sporangia. The prothallus is the small, short-lived haploid gametophyte, and protonema is the young gametophyte stage of mosses.

questions.s: In alternation of generations, haploid spores are produced by the
questions.e: The diploid sporophyte has spore mother cells that divide by meiosis to give haploid spores, each of which grows into a gametophyte. Fertilisation produces the diploid zygote, not spores.

questions.s: In plants with alternation of generations, gametes are produced by mitosis rather than meiosis because
o: the gametophyte that forms them is already haploid
gametes must be diploid to fuse
meiosis takes place only in animals
questions.e: The gametophyte grows from a haploid spore, so its cells are already haploid and simple mitosis gives haploid gametes. Meiosis happened earlier, during spore formation in the sporophyte, so the chromosome number is halved only once in the cycle.

questions.s: Gymnosperms are so named because their
o: seeds are not enclosed in an ovary
spores are all of one kind
questions.e: Gymnosperm means naked seed: the ovules lie exposed on the surface of cone scales and are not enclosed in an ovary, so no fruit forms. Needle-like leaves are common in conifers but are not what the name refers to.

questions.s: In angiosperms, the endosperm formed by double fertilisation is
questions.e: One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, and the second fuses with the two haploid polar nuclei (or the diploid secondary nucleus), giving a 3n endosperm nucleus. Diploid is the zygote, not the endosperm.

questions.s: Which plant shows heterospory, producing microspores and megaspores, an important step towards the seed habit?
questions.e: Selaginella forms small microspores and large megaspores in separate sporangia, and the female gametophyte develops inside the megaspore, as in seed plants. Adiantum, Equisetum and Psilotum are homosporous, producing only one kind of spore.

questions.s: Potato, tomato and brinjal belong to the family
questions.e: These vegetables are members of Solanaceae, which has five-part flowers with fused petals and a two-chambered ovary. Fabaceae includes peas and beans, Rosaceae roses and apples, and Poaceae the grasses and cereals.

questions.s: Plants of the family Fabaceae (pea family) improve soil fertility because their roots
o: form mycorrhizae that make nitrates from lightning
questions.e: Root nodules of legumes such as pea, gram and beans house Rhizobium bacteria, which convert atmospheric N₂ into ammonia that the plant uses; the rest enriches the soil. Plants themselves cannot use nitrogen gas directly.

questions.s: Which feature indicates that a flowering plant is a monocot?
o: Two cotyledons and a tap root
Net venation and flower parts in fives
Parallel leaf venation and flower parts in threes
Vascular bundles arranged in a single ring in the stem
questions.e: Monocots such as wheat and maize have one cotyledon, parallel veins, scattered vascular bundles and floral parts in threes. Two cotyledons, net venation, tap roots and a ring of bundles are dicot features.

questions.s: Plants that possess specialised conducting tissues, xylem and phloem, are grouped together as
questions.e: Tracheophytes (vascular plants) include ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms; their lignified xylem carries water and also gives support. Bryophytes have no true xylem or phloem, which keeps them small and close to the ground.

questions.s: Collar cells (choanocytes), which create water currents and trap food, are characteristic of the phylum
questions.e: Sponges (Porifera) have choanocytes lining their canals; the beating flagella draw water in through the ostia and the collars trap food particles. Cnidarians have stinging cells instead.

questions.s: Stinging cells (cnidocytes) containing nematocysts are found in
questions.e: Cnidocytes discharge nematocysts to paralyse prey and give the phylum Cnidaria its name. Sponges, earthworms and snails have no stinging cells.

questions.s: A diploblastic animal is one whose body develops from
questions.e: Diploblastic animals such as Hydra have two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with a jelly-like mesoglea between them. Animals with all three layers, including mesoderm, are triploblastic.

questions.s: Which phylum consists of triploblastic animals that have no body cavity (acoelomates)?
questions.e: Flatworms such as the liver fluke and tapeworm have three germ layers, but the space between gut and body wall is filled with mesenchyme. Nematodes have a pseudocoelom, while annelids and arthropods have a true coelom.

questions.s: Roundworms such as Ascaris are pseudocoelomates because their body cavity
o: is lined by mesoderm on both of its sides
is not completely lined by mesoderm
questions.e: A pseudocoelom lies between the mesoderm of the body wall and the endoderm of the gut, so mesoderm lines it on one side only. A true coelom is lined by mesoderm on both sides, and a cavity filled with tissue describes acoelomates.

questions.s: The earthworm shows a true coelom and a body divided into similar repeated rings. It belongs to the phylum
questions.e: Annelids have metameric segmentation, in which the body is divided into similar segments, and a true coelom. Nematodes are unsegmented, and arthropods are segmented but have jointed legs and an exoskeleton.

questions.s: Jointed appendages and an exoskeleton containing chitin are characteristic features of
questions.e: Insects, spiders, crabs and centipedes (arthropods) have a chitinous exoskeleton that they moult and jointed legs. Annelids have no jointed legs and molluscs have a soft body, usually with a shell.

questions.s: A soft unsegmented body covered by a mantle, which usually secretes a shell, is a feature of the phylum
questions.e: Snails, mussels and octopus are molluscs; the mantle is a fold of the body wall that secretes the shell. Echinoderms have an internal skeleton of calcareous plates, not a mantle.

questions.s: A water vascular system with tube feet, used for movement and feeding, is found in
questions.e: Echinoderms such as starfish and sea urchins move water through canals into tube feet, which work by hydraulic pressure. Jellyfish swim by contracting their bell, and octopus uses jet propulsion and arms.

questions.s: Which set of features is found in all chordates at some stage of their life?
o: Notochord, ventral solid nerve cord and a chitin exoskeleton
Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal slits
Dorsal heart, ventral nerve cord and gills
questions.e: Every chordate has a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits at least in the embryo. A backbone is found only in vertebrates, and a ventral solid nerve cord is typical of non-chordates such as annelids and arthropods.

questions.s: Bilateral symmetry in animals is closely linked with
o: cephalisation, the concentration of sense organs at the front end
the absence of a nervous system
questions.e: A bilaterally symmetrical animal moves head first, so sense organs and nerve cells concentrate at the front (cephalisation). Radial symmetry suits sessile or slow animals such as sea anemones, which meet the environment equally from all sides.

questions.s: Echinoderms are considered more closely related to chordates than to arthropods because both echinoderms and chordates
o: have jointed limbs and a chitin skeleton
are deuterostomes, in which the blastopore becomes the anus
questions.e: In deuterostomes the first embryonic opening (blastopore) becomes the anus and the mouth forms later; arthropods, annelids and molluscs are protostomes, in which the blastopore becomes the mouth. Adult echinoderms are radial, but their larvae are bilateral and they are triploblastic.

questions.s: Experiments using the heavy oxygen isotope ¹⁸O showed that the oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from
questions.e: When ¹⁸O was supplied in water, the released O₂ was labelled; when it was supplied in CO₂, it was not. So O₂ comes from the splitting (photolysis) of water, while the oxygen of CO₂ ends up in sugar and water.

questions.s: Leaves look green because chlorophyll
o: absorbs mainly blue and red light and reflects green
questions.e: Chlorophylls a and b absorb strongly in the blue and red regions, so the green light is mostly reflected or transmitted and reaches our eyes. Green light being absorbed is the reverse of what happens.

questions.s: The reaction centre chlorophylls of photosystem I and photosystem II are, respectively,
questions.e: The numbers are the wavelengths in nm at which each reaction centre absorbs best: P700 for photosystem I and P680 for photosystem II. Swapping them is the common error, since PSII acts first in the Z-scheme despite its number.

questions.s: The splitting of water (photolysis) during the light reactions supplies electrons directly to
questions.e: When P680 of photosystem II loses electrons to the transport chain, it replaces them by splitting water, which releases O₂ and H⁺. Photosystem I gets its electrons from PSII through the chain, not from water.

questions.s: In C₃ plants, the first stable product formed when CO₂ is fixed in the Calvin cycle is
questions.e: Rubisco joins CO₂ to the 5-carbon RuBP, giving an unstable 6-carbon compound that splits at once into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (PGA). RuBP is the CO₂ acceptor, and oxaloacetate is the first product in C₄ plants.

questions.s: In the Calvin cycle, the ATP and NADPH needed to fix 6 molecules of CO₂ into one glucose molecule are
questions.e: Each CO₂ fixed needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH (2 ATP and 2 NADPH to reduce two PGA, and 1 ATP to regenerate RuBP), so 6 CO₂ need 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH. Reversing the two numbers is the usual slip.

questions.s: Cyclic photophosphorylation differs from non-cyclic photophosphorylation because it produces
o: NADPH only, without any ATP or oxygen
ATP only, without NADPH or oxygen
questions.e: In the cyclic path, electrons from photosystem I return to it through the transport chain, making ATP but no NADPH; since water is not split, no oxygen is released. The non-cyclic path through both photosystems gives ATP, NADPH and O₂.

questions.s: A plant in bright light at 25 °C photosynthesises faster when the CO₂ concentration around it is increased. Before the increase, the limiting factor was
questions.e: By Blackman's law of limiting factors, the rate is controlled by the factor in shortest supply; since raising CO₂ alone increased the rate, CO₂ was limiting. If light were limiting, extra CO₂ would have had no effect.

questions.s: Glycolysis, the first stage of cellular respiration, takes place in the
questions.e: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules using enzymes in the cytoplasm (cytosol) and needs no oxygen. The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane.

questions.s: The net products of glycolysis from one molecule of glucose are
questions.e: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses 2 ATP at the start, giving a net 2 ATP, along with 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate. Counting 4 ATP forgets the 2 used in the investment step, and acetyl CoA is formed later in the mitochondrion.

questions.s: In the Krebs cycle, acetyl CoA (2 carbons) combines with oxaloacetate (4 carbons) to form
questions.e: The 2-carbon acetyl group joins 4-carbon oxaloacetate to give 6-carbon citric acid, which is then oxidised step by step, releasing 2 CO₂ and regenerating oxaloacetate. Pyruvate is the product of glycolysis, not of the Krebs cycle.

questions.s: The final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration is
questions.e: At the end of the chain, cytochrome oxidase passes electrons to oxygen, which combines with H⁺ to form water. NAD⁺ carries electrons into the chain, and pyruvate is the acceptor in anaerobic (lactic acid) respiration, not in the chain.

questions.s: During vigorous exercise, human muscle cells short of oxygen convert pyruvate into
questions.e: In anaerobic conditions muscle cells reduce pyruvate to lactic acid, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. Ethanol and CO₂ are the products of fermentation in yeast.

questions.s: Photorespiration lowers the efficiency of photosynthesis in C₃ plants on hot, dry days because
o: chlorophyll is destroyed by strong light
the light reactions stop producing ATP
rubisco combines with O₂ instead of CO₂ when stomata close
glucose is converted into starch too quickly
questions.e: When stomata close to save water, O₂ builds up and CO₂ falls inside the leaf; rubisco then adds O₂ to RuBP, and the product is broken down with release of CO₂ and no sugar gain. C₄ plants avoid this by concentrating CO₂ around rubisco.

questions.s: According to the chemiosmotic theory, ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane makes ATP using energy from
o: electrons passing directly through the ATP synthase enzyme itself
the direct breakdown of glucose in the matrix
H⁺ ions flowing back into the matrix down their gradient
questions.e: The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space; the H⁺ then flow back through ATP synthase, which uses this flow to join ADP and phosphate. Electrons do not pass through ATP synthase itself.

questions.s: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant and Venus flytrap trap insects mainly to obtain
questions.e: These plants are green and make their own sugar by photosynthesis, but they grow in nitrogen-poor soils, so they digest insects to obtain nitrogen. They do not depend on insects for energy.

questions.s: The digestion of starch begins in the mouth by the action of
questions.e: Salivary glands secrete amylase (ptyalin), which starts breaking starch into maltose while food is chewed. Pepsin acts on proteins in the stomach, and trypsin and lipase work in the small intestine.

questions.s: In the stomach, the inactive enzyme pepsinogen is converted into active pepsin by
questions.e: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and parietal cells secrete HCl, which converts it into pepsin; pepsin itself then activates more pepsinogen. Enterokinase activates trypsinogen in the small intestine, not pepsinogen.

questions.s: Bile helps the digestion of fats because it
o: emulsifies fats into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
questions.e: Bile, made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder, contains bile salts but no digestive enzymes; it breaks fat into small droplets so pancreatic lipase can act faster. Thinking bile contains lipase is the common mistake.

questions.s: In the villi of the small intestine, digested fats are mainly absorbed into the
questions.e: Fatty acids and glycerol are reformed into fats inside the epithelial cells and enter the lacteal, a lymph vessel in the centre of each villus. Sugars and amino acids enter the blood capillaries and travel through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

questions.s: Most peptic ulcers of the stomach and duodenum are now known to be linked with infection by the bacterium
questions.e: Helicobacter pylori survives in the stomach lining and weakens its protective mucus, so acid and pepsin damage the wall. E. coli is a normal gut bacterium, and Vibrio cholerae causes cholera with watery diarrhoea, not ulcers.

questions.s: Stomata open in light because potassium ions are actively moved into the guard cells, which
o: raises their water potential, so water leaves and they become flaccid
makes the guard cells thinner on the inner wall
converts sugar into starch inside them
lowers their water potential, so water enters and they become turgid
questions.e: Entry of K⁺ makes the guard cell sap more concentrated, so water moves in by osmosis; the thick inner walls bend as the cells swell and the pore opens. Water leaving makes the cells flaccid and closes the stoma, which is what happens in darkness.

questions.s: In human lungs, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place across the walls of the
questions.e: Alveoli are tiny air sacs with very thin walls, a huge total surface and a dense network of capillaries, ideal for diffusion. The trachea and bronchi only conduct air, and the pleura surrounds the lungs.

questions.s: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as hydrogencarbonate ions, which form mainly
o: in the plasma, without any enzyme
inside red blood cells, by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase
on the haem group of haemoglobin
inside white blood cells, by lipase
questions.e: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells rapidly converts CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which ionises into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the HCO₃⁻ then diffuses into the plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (chloride shift). Only a small fraction of CO₂ binds haemoglobin, and it binds the protein part, not the haem.

questions.s: Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it
o: combines with haemoglobin far more firmly than oxygen does
questions.e: CO binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which is very stable, so less haemoglobin is free to carry O₂ and the tissues suffer oxygen lack. It does not burst red cells.

questions.s: In emphysema, breathing becomes difficult mainly because
o: the bronchi are blocked by a tumour
the pleural cavity fills with air
walls of the alveoli break down, reducing the surface for gas exchange
questions.e: Long exposure to smoke damages the elastic alveolar walls, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large sacs with much less surface area. A blocking tumour describes lung cancer, and air in the pleural cavity is a collapsed lung.

questions.s: In flowering plants, water and dissolved minerals move up from the roots mainly through the
questions.e: Xylem vessels and tracheids form continuous dead tubes that carry water and minerals upward. Phloem carries sugars and other organic food in translocation, which is the usual confusion.

questions.s: According to the cohesion-tension theory, water rises to the top of a tall tree mainly because
o: transpiration from leaves pulls a continuous column of water molecules held together by cohesion
root pressure pushes water to the top
phloem pumps water upward using ATP
water is absorbed directly by the leaves
questions.e: Evaporation from leaf cells creates tension that pulls water up the xylem, and hydrogen bonding (cohesion) keeps the column unbroken. Root pressure exists but is far too weak to lift water up a tall tree.

questions.s: According to the pressure-flow (mass flow) hypothesis, phloem sap moves from a leaf to a root because
o: xylem pulls the sap down by transpiration
sugar loading at the leaf draws in water, building pressure that pushes sap towards the root where sugar is removed
gravity carries the sap down to the root
questions.e: Sucrose loaded into sieve tubes at the source lowers water potential, so water enters from the xylem and hydrostatic pressure rises; at the sink sugar is unloaded, water leaves and pressure falls, so sap flows from high to low pressure. This is why phloem can carry sap upwards too, ruling out gravity.

questions.s: The natural pacemaker that starts each heartbeat is the
questions.e: The SA node in the wall of the right atrium sends out impulses that spread over both atria, making them contract. The AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres pass the impulse on to the ventricles but do not start it.

questions.s: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the heart through the
o: pulmonary arteries into the right atrium
venae cavae into the right atrium
pulmonary veins into the left atrium
questions.e: Pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood, and they open into the left atrium. Pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.s: Antibodies are produced by
o: plasma cells formed from B lymphocytes
questions.e: When a B lymphocyte meets its matching antigen it multiplies and forms plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody. Helper T cells regulate the immune response, and neutrophils destroy microbes by phagocytosis.

questions.s: A person bitten by a snake is injected with antiserum containing ready-made antibodies against the venom. This gives
questions.e: The antibodies are made by another animal and given by injection, so the immunity is passive (the body makes none itself) and artificial; it works at once but lasts only a short time. A vaccine would give artificial active immunity, and antibodies crossing the placenta give natural passive immunity.

questions.s: Lymph collected from the tissues is finally returned to the blood when the thoracic duct empties into the
questions.e: Lymph vessels collect excess tissue fluid and drain it through lymph nodes into the thoracic duct, which opens into the left subclavian vein near the heart. This keeps blood volume steady and prevents oedema.

questions.s: The chamber of the human heart with the thickest muscular wall is the
questions.e: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aorta to the whole body, so it must produce the highest pressure. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, so its wall is thinner.

questions.s: A freshwater bony fish lives in water that is hypotonic to its body fluids. To osmoregulate it
o: drinks large amounts of water and excretes salt through its gills
produces very little, highly concentrated urine
stores urea in its blood to raise its osmotic pressure
excretes large volumes of dilute urine
questions.e: Water keeps entering the fish by osmosis, so its kidneys remove the excess as plenty of dilute urine, while the gills actively take up salts. Drinking water and excreting salt is what a marine bony fish does, and storing urea is the shark's method.

questions.s: A marine bony fish loses water by osmosis to the sea. It makes up for this by
o: drinking sea water and excreting excess salt through its gills
absorbing large amounts of water through its skin from the sea around it
producing large volumes of dilute urine
storing extra urea in its blood
questions.e: Sea water is hypertonic to its body fluids, so the fish drinks it and chloride cells in the gills actively remove the extra salt; it makes only a little urine. Producing large volumes of dilute urine would make the water loss worse.

questions.s: In humans, the main nitrogenous waste is urea, which is made in the
questions.e: Liver cells convert toxic ammonia from excess amino acids into urea through the ornithine cycle. The kidneys only filter urea out of the blood and the bladder stores the urine.

questions.s: Birds, reptiles and insects excrete mainly uric acid because it
o: is the most toxic nitrogenous waste
dissolves easily in large amounts of water
needs very little water for its removal
is the cheapest waste to make in terms of energy and requires no enzymes
questions.e: Uric acid is nearly insoluble and of low toxicity, so it can be excreted as a paste with very little water, which also suits development inside a shelled egg. Ammonia is the most toxic and needs the most water, which is why mainly aquatic animals excrete it.

questions.s: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
questions.e: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, each with a glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, tubules and loop of Henle that together form urine. The glomerulus is only the capillary knot at the start of a nephron.

questions.s: In the nephron, ultrafiltration of blood takes place from the
o: loop of Henle into the medulla
questions.e: High blood pressure in the glomerulus, because its outgoing arteriole is narrower than the incoming one, forces water and small solutes into Bowman's capsule. Large proteins and blood cells stay behind; the other regions handle reabsorption and secretion.

questions.s: In a healthy person, almost all the glucose in the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed in the
o: Bowman's capsule, before reaching the tubule
questions.e: Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have microvilli and many mitochondria and actively reabsorb all glucose and amino acids. Glucose appears in the urine only when the blood level is so high that these carriers are saturated, as in untreated diabetes.

questions.s: When a person is dehydrated, the urine becomes small in volume and concentrated because
o: less ADH is secreted, making the collecting ducts impermeable to water
more ADH is secreted, making collecting ducts more permeable to water
questions.e: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect concentrated blood and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH; the collecting ducts then let more water pass back into the salty medulla. Less ADH would produce a large volume of dilute urine.

questions.s: Desert mammals such as the kangaroo rat can produce very concentrated urine mainly because they have
o: no glomeruli and so no filtration
very long loops of Henle that build a high salt concentration in the medulla
collecting ducts that cannot be affected by ADH
questions.e: The longer the loop of Henle, the steeper the salt gradient that the countercurrent mechanism creates in the medulla, so more water can be drawn out of the collecting ducts. Collecting ducts that ignore ADH would produce dilute urine instead.

questions.s: On a hot day in Karachi, the skin helps lose heat from the body mainly by
o: narrowing of skin arterioles and shivering
raising the body hairs and trapping a warm layer of air
increasing the metabolic rate of the liver
widening of skin arterioles and secretion of sweat
questions.e: Vasodilation brings more warm blood near the surface to lose heat, and evaporation of sweat removes latent heat. Vasoconstriction, shivering and raised hairs are responses to cold.

questions.s: The temperature-regulating centre (thermostat) of the human body is located in the
questions.e: The hypothalamus monitors blood temperature and starts responses such as sweating or shivering. The thyroid raises metabolic rate under its control, but does not sense temperature.

questions.s: The hip and shoulder joints, which allow movement in many directions, are
questions.e: The rounded head of one bone fits into a cup of another, allowing rotation and movement in all planes. Hinge joints such as the elbow and knee move in one plane only.

questions.s: According to the sliding filament theory, when a skeletal muscle fibre contracts,
o: the I-band and H-zone shorten while the A-band stays the same length
the A-band shortens while the I-band stays the same
both the actin and the myosin filaments themselves become much shorter
the Z-lines move further apart from each other
questions.e: Actin filaments slide over myosin towards the centre of the sarcomere, so the Z-lines come closer and the regions containing only actin (I-band) or only myosin (H-zone) shrink. The A-band equals the length of the myosin filaments, which do not change.

questions.s: In skeletal muscle, contraction is triggered when calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
o: bind to myosin heads and break ATP
close the channels in the sarcolemma
bind to troponin, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin
questions.e: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin; myosin heads can then attach, form cross-bridges and pull. ATP is split by the myosin head itself, not by calcium.

questions.s: In plants, sclerenchyma gives mechanical support because its cells
o: are living cells with thin cellulose walls
have thick lignified walls and are usually dead at maturity
are living cells that are thickened only at their corners with pectin
stay turgid by filling with water
questions.e: Fibres and sclereids have heavily lignified secondary walls, giving strength even after the cell contents die. Living cells thickened at the corners describe collenchyma, and support by turgor is typical of parenchyma.

questions.s: A shoot tip lit from one side bends towards the light because auxin
o: accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more
is destroyed on the shaded side, so cells on the lit side grow faster
moves to the lit side and makes those cells divide
stops all growth on the lit side by closing stomata
questions.e: Auxin moves away from light, so the shaded side gets more of it; its cells elongate faster and the shoot curves towards the light (positive phototropism). Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots, not closing of stomata, which is the role of abscisic acid.

questions.s: The plant hormone that causes rapid stem elongation (bolting) and helps break seed dormancy in cereals is
questions.e: Gibberellins promote internode elongation and, in germinating cereal grains, trigger amylase production that mobilises stored starch. Abscisic acid has the opposite effect, maintaining dormancy.

questions.s: During drought, the hormone that causes stomata to close and reduces water loss is
questions.e: Water stress raises abscisic acid levels in leaves; it makes guard cells lose K⁺ and water, so the stomata close. It is called the stress hormone, while cytokinins delay ageing and promote cell division.

questions.s: The gaseous plant hormone that speeds up the ripening of fruits such as bananas and mangoes is
questions.e: Ethylene (ethene) is a gas released by ripening fruit, which is why one ripe fruit hastens the ripening of others stored with it. Auxin and gibberellin mainly control growth.

questions.s: Nerve impulses travel faster along myelinated neurons because
o: myelin itself carries the electric current along the axon
the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
myelinated axons have no sodium channels at all
the axon is thinner under the myelin sheath
questions.e: Myelin made by Schwann cells insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier) and the impulse leaps between them (saltatory conduction). Myelin is an insulator and does not conduct the current itself.

questions.s: The sodium-potassium pump helps maintain the resting potential of a neuron by moving, for each ATP used,
o: 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into it
2 Na⁺ out of the cell and 3 K⁺ into it
3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out of it
equal numbers of Na⁺ and K⁺ in both directions
questions.e: The pump expels three sodium ions and brings in two potassium ions per cycle, so more positive charge leaves than enters, helping keep the inside negative at about −70 mV. Swapping the numbers would make the inside more positive.

questions.s: The rising phase (depolarisation) of an action potential is caused by
o: rapid outflow of K⁺ ions from the axon
inflow of Cl⁻ ions into the axon
rapid inflow of Na⁺ ions into the axon
the sodium-potassium pump working faster than usual
questions.e: A stimulus opens voltage-gated sodium channels, and Na⁺ rushes in, reversing the potential to about +40 mV. The outflow of K⁺ comes next and causes repolarisation.

questions.s: At a chemical synapse, an impulse can pass in only one direction because
o: the synaptic cleft allows ions to flow only one way
the postsynaptic neuron has no sodium channels
acetylcholine is destroyed in the presynaptic knob
only the presynaptic knob releases neurotransmitter and only the postsynaptic membrane has its receptors
questions.e: Vesicles of neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine are found only in the presynaptic terminal, and the receptors for it are on the postsynaptic membrane, so transmission is one-way. Acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, not in the knob.

questions.s: In a reflex arc, the neuron that carries impulses from the spinal cord to the effector muscle is the
questions.e: The path is receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron, effector. Sensory neurons carry impulses towards the spinal cord, not away from it.

questions.s: Maintaining balance and coordinating smooth, precise movements is the main function of the
questions.e: The cerebellum receives information from muscles, joints and the inner ear and fine-tunes movements. The cerebrum starts voluntary movements and the medulla controls breathing and heart rate.

questions.s: The part of the brain that controls breathing rate, heart rate and blood pressure is the
questions.e: The medulla in the hindbrain contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centres, which work without conscious control. Damage there is often fatal, while the cerebellum controls balance.

questions.s: Insulin, which lowers blood glucose level, is secreted by the
o: α-cells of the islets of Langerhans
β-cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.e: Insulin from β-cells makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen. α-cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose, so the two cell types are easily swapped.

questions.s: A lack of iodine in the diet often leads to an enlarged thyroid gland (goitre) because iodine is needed to make
questions.e: Thyroxine contains iodine; when it cannot be made, low thyroxine allows high TSH from the pituitary, which keeps stimulating the thyroid to enlarge. Insulin, adrenaline and growth hormone contain no iodine.

questions.s: When the level of thyroxine in the blood rises above normal, the secretion of TSH by the anterior pituitary
o: increases, an example of positive feedback
decreases, an example of positive feedback
stays the same, as the two are unrelated
decreases, an example of negative feedback
questions.e: High thyroxine inhibits the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so less TSH is released and thyroxine output falls back to normal. Feedback that reverses the change is negative; positive feedback would push the level even higher.

questions.s: Newly hatched ducklings follow the first moving object they see, even a human, and keep following it. This behaviour is called
questions.e: Imprinting is rapid learning during a short sensitive period early in life, studied by Konrad Lorenz with geese. Habituation is learning to ignore a repeated harmless stimulus, which does not fit this case.

questions.s: Farmers grow new potato plants from the "eyes" of potatoes. This is vegetative propagation by
questions.e: A potato is a swollen underground stem; its eyes are buds that grow into new shoots. Sweet potato is a root tuber, onion is a bulb, and runners are creeping stems above the soil, as in strawberry.

questions.s: In honeybees, male drones develop from unfertilised eggs. This type of reproduction is called
questions.e: Parthenogenesis is the development of an egg into a new individual without fertilisation, so drones are haploid. Budding and fragmentation produce new individuals from body parts, not from eggs.

questions.s: In the human testis, testosterone is secreted mainly by the
questions.e: Leydig cells lie between the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone under the control of LH. Sertoli cells, inside the tubules, nourish the developing sperm, and the epididymis stores sperm.

questions.s: In humans, fertilisation of the ovum normally takes place in the
questions.e: After ovulation the secondary oocyte is swept into the oviduct, where it meets sperm and is fertilised; the zygote then travels to the uterus and implants there. The uterus is the site of implantation, not usually of fertilisation.

questions.s: In the menstrual cycle, ovulation is triggered by a sudden surge in the secretion of
questions.e: Rising oestrogen from the growing follicle causes the anterior pituitary to release a burst of LH around the middle of the cycle, which makes the mature follicle burst. Progesterone rises only after ovulation, from the corpus luteum.

questions.s: After ovulation, the corpus luteum mainly secretes
o: testosterone, which stops menstruation for several months
progesterone, which keeps the uterine lining thick
questions.e: The corpus luteum forms from the empty follicle and secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen), which maintains the endometrium for a possible pregnancy. FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary, not the ovary.

questions.s: If the ovum is not fertilised, menstruation begins at the end of the cycle because
o: the corpus luteum degenerates and the progesterone level falls
FSH secretion stops completely and permanently
oestrogen rises sharply and directly breaks down the endometrium
LH stays at its highest level
questions.e: Without a pregnancy hormone to maintain it, the corpus luteum breaks down after about two weeks; falling progesterone can no longer support the thick endometrium, which is shed. The fall in progesterone also releases its inhibition of FSH, so a new cycle starts.

questions.s: Syphilis, a sexually transmitted disease, is caused by
questions.e: Syphilis is caused by a spiral bacterium, Treponema pallidum, and is treatable with antibiotics if detected early. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea, another bacterial STD, which is the usual confusion.

questions.s: In a vertebrate embryo, the brain and spinal cord develop from the
questions.e: The neural tube forms when the ectoderm above the notochord folds inwards, giving the brain and spinal cord. Mesoderm forms muscle, bone and blood, and endoderm forms the lining of the gut.

questions.s: The correct order of stages in early animal development is
questions.e: The zygote first divides by cleavage into a hollow ball (blastula); gastrulation then forms the germ layers, and only after that do organs form. Germ layers must exist before organs can arise from them.

questions.s: In experiments with amphibian embryos, Spemann and Mangold found that a graft of the dorsal lip of the blastopore could make the host form a second embryo. This tissue is called the
questions.e: The dorsal lip of the blastopore induces the overlying ectoderm to form a neural tube, so a grafted piece organises a second body axis; Spemann named it the primary organiser. The yolk plug is just the yolk cells visible through the blastopore.

questions.s: In humans, which organ shows a notable ability to regenerate lost tissue?
questions.e: Liver cells can divide again after injury, so even after part of the liver is removed it regrows to nearly its full mass. Nerve cells of the brain and cardiac muscle cells rarely divide, so damage there is mostly permanent.

questions.s: Pollination in flowering plants is the transfer of pollen grains from the
o: stigma to the ovule inside the ovary
questions.e: Pollen is made in the anther and must land on a receptive stigma, either of the same flower (self-pollination) or of another (cross-pollination). Growth of the pollen tube down the style to the ovule happens afterwards and is not pollination.

questions.s: In spermatogenesis, one primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis to produce
o: one spermatid and three polar bodies
questions.e: The two meiotic divisions of one primary spermatocyte give four haploid spermatids, which mature into four sperms. Formation of polar bodies, with most cytoplasm kept in one cell, happens in oogenesis, not in spermatogenesis.

questions.s: Early in pregnancy, the corpus luteum does not degenerate because the embryo and placenta secrete
questions.e: hCG from the developing chorion acts like LH and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta can make enough itself. Its detection in urine is the basis of pregnancy tests. Oxytocin causes uterine contractions at birth, and prolactin stimulates milk production.

questions.s: The constricted region of a chromosome that holds the two sister chromatids together is the
questions.e: The centromere (primary constriction) joins sister chromatids and carries the kinetochores, where spindle fibres attach during division. Telomeres are the protective ends of the chromosome.

questions.s: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) and then on ordinary ¹⁴N. Their results showed that DNA replication is
questions.e: After one generation in ¹⁴N all DNA was of intermediate density, so each new molecule had one old and one new strand. Conservative replication would have produced one fully heavy and one fully light band instead.

questions.s: In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, E. coli with only ¹⁵N-DNA is grown for two generations in a ¹⁴N medium. The DNA then consists of
o: one quarter heavy (¹⁵N-¹⁵N) and three quarters light
questions.e: After generation 1 every molecule is hybrid. Each hybrid then separates into one ¹⁵N and one ¹⁴N strand, and both get new ¹⁴N partners, giving one hybrid and one light molecule, so 50 % of each. All hybrid is the result after only one generation.

questions.s: During DNA replication, the short Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand are joined together by
questions.e: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5′ to 3′ direction, so the lagging strand is made in short pieces; DNA ligase seals the gaps between them. Helicase unwinds the double helix and primase lays down the RNA primers.

questions.s: A DNA template strand has the base sequence 3′-TACGGA-5′. The mRNA transcribed from it is
questions.e: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, giving 5′-AUGCCU-3′. 5′-ATGCCT-3′ has the right pairing but contains thymine, which is not found in RNA.

questions.s: With four different bases read three at a time, the total number of possible codons is
questions.e: The number of triplets is 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64. Of these, 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons, which is why 61 is a tempting wrong answer.

questions.s: The start codon AUG, which begins translation, codes for the amino acid
questions.e: AUG is the initiation codon and also codes for methionine, so most new polypeptides begin with methionine. It is read by the initiator tRNA carrying methionine at the start of translation.

questions.s: Which of the following mRNA codons does not code for any amino acid and stops translation?
questions.e: UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons; no tRNA matches them, so release factors free the polypeptide. AUG is the start codon, GUA codes for valine and UUU for phenylalanine.

questions.s: Which mutation near the start of a gene is most likely to change every amino acid after it?
o: Substitution of three bases in one codon
questions.e: Deleting a single base shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is read wrongly (frameshift). A substitution changes at most one codon, and deleting three adjacent bases removes about one amino acid but keeps the frame.

questions.s: Sickle-cell anaemia results from a point mutation in the gene for the β-chain of haemoglobin, in which
o: valine is replaced by glutamic acid
glutamic acid is replaced by valine
the β-chain is not made at all
questions.e: A single base substitution (A to T in the DNA) changes the sixth codon so that valine replaces glutamic acid. The altered haemoglobin crystallises at low oxygen and distorts red cells into sickle shapes.

questions.s: Down syndrome is caused by
o: the loss of one X chromosome
an extra X chromosome in males
a mutation on the Y chromosome
questions.e: Most cases result from non-disjunction during meiosis, giving a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21, so the child has trisomy 21 and 47 chromosomes. Loss of an X gives Turner syndrome and an extra X in males gives Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.s: During mitosis, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles in
questions.e: At anaphase the centromeres split and the spindle fibres pull the chromatids, now separate chromosomes, to opposite poles. In metaphase they are only lined up at the equator.

questions.s: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes takes place during
questions.e: In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis), and non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata. Homologues are not paired in meiosis II or in mitosis, so crossing over cannot occur there.

questions.s: DNA is replicated during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.e: S stands for synthesis: each chromosome is copied to form two sister chromatids. G₁ is growth before replication, G₂ is preparation for division, and M is mitosis itself.

questions.s: A human primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. Each of the two cells formed at the end of meiosis I contains
o: 23 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids
23 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid
46 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid
46 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids
questions.e: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so the number halves to 23, but sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase II. Single-chromatid chromosomes appear only after meiosis II.

questions.s: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). A cross Tt × Tt gives offspring in the phenotypic ratio
questions.e: The offspring genotypes are TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1; TT and Tt are both tall, so the phenotype ratio is 3 : 1. The 1 : 1 ratio is from a test cross, Tt × tt.

questions.s: Bilal crosses a tall pea plant with a dwarf (tt) plant and gets about half tall and half dwarf offspring. The genotype of the tall parent is
o: TT or Tt, which cannot be told apart
questions.e: This is a test cross: a TT parent would give all tall (Tt) offspring, while Tt × tt gives Tt and tt in a 1 : 1 ratio. Appearance of dwarf plants shows the tall parent must carry the recessive allele.

questions.s: In a cross between two pea plants both heterozygous for two independently assorting genes (AaBb × AaBb), the fraction of offspring with the genotype aabb is
questions.e: Each gene independently gives aa with probability 1/4 and bb with probability 1/4, so aabb = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. 9/16 is the fraction showing both dominant traits, and 3/16 each of the two mixed classes.

questions.s: In four o'clock plants, red-flowered (RR) × white-flowered (rr) gives all pink F₁. Selfing the F₁ gives an F₂ phenotypic ratio of
questions.e: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote Rr is pink, so each genotype has its own colour and RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1 appears directly as 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. A 3 : 1 ratio would mean red was fully dominant.

questions.s: A man with blood group A (genotype IAi) and a woman with blood group B (IBi) have a child. The probability that the child has blood group O is
questions.e: Group O needs genotype ii, so each parent must pass on i, each with probability 1/2, giving 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Answering 0 forgets that both parents carry the recessive allele i.

questions.s: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man (XᴴY). The probability that any son of theirs will be haemophilic is
questions.e: A son gets his Y from the father and one X from the mother, who passes Xʰ half the time, so each son has a 1/2 chance of being haemophilic. 1/4 is the chance for any child (son or daughter) before the sex is known.

questions.s: According to Morgan's work on linkage, the frequency of crossing over between two genes on the same chromosome is greater when the genes are
questions.e: A chiasma is more likely to form somewhere between two genes the greater the distance between them, so recombination frequency rises with distance; this is the basis of gene mapping. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently rather than by crossing over.

questions.s: Restriction endonucleases, such as EcoRI, are enzymes that
o: cut DNA at specific base sequences
join broken DNA fragments together end to end
questions.e: Each restriction enzyme recognises a particular short sequence (EcoRI recognises GAATTC) and cuts DNA only there. Joining fragments is the work of DNA ligase, which is the common mix-up.

questions.s: In making recombinant DNA, the gene and the plasmid are cut with the same restriction enzyme so that
o: the plasmid loses all its genes
they have matching sticky ends that can base-pair
the gene is copied many times at once inside the tube
no DNA ligase is needed afterwards
questions.e: Enzymes such as EcoRI make staggered cuts, leaving short single-stranded ends; ends made by the same enzyme are complementary and pair up. DNA ligase is still needed to seal the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.s: The small circular DNA molecules of bacteria, widely used as vectors in genetic engineering, are called
questions.e: Plasmids replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and often carry antibiotic-resistance genes, which help identify cells that took them up. Mesosomes are infoldings of the bacterial membrane, not DNA.

questions.s: The DNA polymerase used in the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) comes from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus because it
o: is not destroyed at the high temperature used to separate DNA strands
questions.e: Each PCR cycle heats DNA to about 95 °C to separate the strands; Taq polymerase from this hot-spring bacterium survives that heat, so fresh enzyme need not be added every cycle. Like other DNA polymerases it still needs primers.

questions.s: Starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, the number of copies of the target DNA after 5 cycles of PCR, assuming perfect doubling, is
questions.e: Each cycle doubles the number of molecules, so after n cycles there are 2ⁿ copies: 2⁵ = 32. 10 assumes two copies are added per cycle, and 64 is 2⁶, one cycle too many.

questions.s: The first approved human gene therapy, in 1990, treated a girl with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) by
o: giving her regular injections of antibiotics
inserting a normal ADA gene into her white blood cells and returning them to her body
replacing all her red blood cells with donor cells
removing the faulty gene from every cell in her body
questions.e: Her T lymphocytes were taken out, given a working copy of the adenosine deaminase gene with a viral vector, and infused back. Gene therapy adds a working gene to some cells; it cannot remove a faulty gene from every cell.

questions.s: Dolly the sheep was cloned by
o: fertilising an egg with two sperms
splitting an early embryo into two halves
injecting a human gene into a fertilised egg
transferring the nucleus of an udder cell into an egg whose nucleus had been removed
questions.e: In somatic cell nuclear transfer, the nucleus from an adult mammary (udder) cell was put into an enucleated egg, which developed into an embryo and was implanted in a surrogate mother. So Dolly was genetically identical to the udder-cell donor, not to the egg donor.

questions.s: Human insulin for diabetic patients is now produced on a large scale by
o: genetically modified bacteria carrying the human insulin gene
extracting it from the pancreas of cattle
questions.e: The human insulin gene is inserted into plasmids and put into bacteria such as E. coli, which then make human insulin. Animal insulin from cattle or pigs was used earlier but differs slightly from human insulin.

questions.s: Bt cotton is resistant to some insect pests because it carries a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis that codes for
o: a protein that makes leaves taste sweet
a protein toxic to insect larvae
a hormone that speeds up flowering
questions.e: The Bt gene produces a crystal (Cry) protein that is harmless to humans but kills insect larvae such as bollworms after they eat the plant. This reduces the need for chemical insecticide sprays.

questions.s: The idea that characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime, through use and disuse of organs, are passed to its offspring was proposed by
questions.e: Lamarck's theory of inheritance of acquired characteristics claimed, for example, that giraffes got long necks by stretching. Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection, and Mendel studied the laws of inheritance.

questions.s: According to Darwin's theory, new species arise mainly because
o: natural selection favours individuals with useful inherited variations
organisms change their bodies by use and disuse
all offspring survive and reproduce equally
mutations occur only when they are needed
questions.e: More offspring are produced than can survive; individuals with favourable heritable variations survive and reproduce more, so these traits spread over generations. Change by use and disuse is Lamarck's view, and mutations occur randomly, not on demand.

questions.s: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9 % of individuals show a recessive trait (aa). The percentage of heterozygous carriers (Aa) is
questions.e: q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7; carriers are 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42, i.e. 42 %. 21 % forgets the factor 2, and 49 % is p², the homozygous dominant fraction.

questions.s: The forelimbs of a human, a whale and a bat look different and have different uses, but have the same basic bone pattern. They are
questions.e: Homologous organs share the same basic structure and embryonic origin but may serve different functions, pointing to a common ancestor (divergent evolution). Analogous organs, such as the wings of insects and birds, do the same job but have different structures.

questions.s: Which of the following is an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
questions.e: Abiotic components are the non-living physical and chemical factors such as temperature, light, water and soil minerals. Producers, consumers and decomposers are all living (biotic) components.

questions.s: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is a
questions.e: Grass is the producer, the grasshopper eats it (primary consumer), and the frog eats the grasshopper, so it is the secondary consumer. The snake, feeding on the frog, is the tertiary consumer.

questions.s: Producers in a grassland store 10 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10 % rule of energy transfer, the energy reaching the tertiary consumers is about
questions.e: Each step passes on about 10 %: primary consumers get 1000 kJ, secondary consumers 100 kJ and tertiary consumers 10 kJ. 100 kJ stops one level too early.

questions.s: Which ecological pyramid is always upright and can never be inverted?
o: Pyramid of numbers in a parasitic chain
questions.e: Energy is lost at every transfer as heat, so each level always has less energy than the one below it. Numbers can be inverted (one tree supports many insects) and biomass can be inverted in some aquatic systems where small phytoplankton reproduce fast.

questions.s: In the nitrogen cycle, bacteria of the genus Nitrosomonas convert
questions.e: Nitrification occurs in two steps: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium to nitrite, then Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate. Nitrate to N₂ is denitrification, and N₂ to ammonia is nitrogen fixation.

questions.s: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere into living organisms mainly by
questions.e: Green plants and algae fix CO₂ into sugars during photosynthesis. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all return CO₂ to the air.

questions.s: On bare rock, the first organisms to colonise and begin forming soil in ecological succession are usually
questions.e: Lichens can survive on bare rock; their acids slowly weather the surface and their remains form a thin soil. Mosses, grasses, shrubs and finally trees follow later as the soil deepens.

questions.s: Succession that begins in a pond, where water is gradually filled with sediment and plants until land vegetation develops, is called a
questions.e: A hydrosere starts in water and passes through floating and reed-swamp stages to marsh and finally woodland. A xerosere starts in a dry place, a lithosere specifically on bare rock, and the climax community is the stable final stage, not the process.

questions.s: The biome with the greatest variety of plant and animal species is the
questions.e: Warm temperatures and heavy rainfall all year allow high productivity and many layers of vegetation, providing many niches. Deserts and tundra have extreme conditions that only a few species can tolerate.

questions.s: A population of bacteria in a flask grows fast at first, then the growth slows and the number levels off. The level at which the number stabilises is the
o: maximum biotic potential of the species
questions.e: Limited food and space, and build-up of wastes, slow the growth, giving an S-shaped (logistic) curve that levels off at the carrying capacity. Biotic potential is the maximum rate at which a population could grow without limits, as seen in the J-shaped part of the curve.

questions.s: Which of the following gases is not a greenhouse gas?
questions.e: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from the Earth's surface; CO₂, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide and CFCs do so. Nitrogen (N₂), the main gas of air, does not absorb infrared and so does not trap heat.

questions.s: The thinning of the ozone layer in the stratosphere is mainly caused by
questions.e: CFCs released from old refrigerators and aerosols release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere, and each can destroy many ozone molecules. CO₂ causes global warming and SO₂ causes acid rain, not ozone depletion.

questions.s: Protecting endangered species, such as the snow leopard, in their natural habitat by declaring national parks is an example of
questions.e: In-situ means on site: the species is protected along with its whole habitat, as in national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. Zoos, botanical gardens and seed banks keep organisms away from their natural habitat, which is ex-situ conservation.

questions.s: Large-scale cutting of forests on hill slopes in northern Pakistan most directly increases
o: the oxygen content of the atmosphere
the number of habitats for wildlife
questions.e: Tree roots bind the soil and the canopy slows rainwater, so after deforestation rain washes topsoil away and runs off quickly, raising flood risk downstream. Deforestation reduces habitats and tends to lower local rainfall.

questions.s: Fertiliser washed from farms into a lake leads to dense algal growth, and soon many fish die. The main reason the fish die is that
o: the algae produce poisonous carbon monoxide
the fertiliser directly poisons the fish
the water becomes too cold for them
bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen
questions.e: Nitrates and phosphates cause an algal bloom (eutrophication); when the algae die, aerobic decomposers multiply and consume dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate. The fertiliser itself is not usually poisonous at these levels.
